Text:
‎{{c1::أبوكَ / أبوكِ}}

Transliteration: {{c1::abuuka / abuuki}}

{{c2::your father}} — to a man / to a woman
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — abuuka / abuuki

Distinguish: -ka to a man, -ki to a woman — the same pair of endings as ismuka / ismuki.

Ex: she went round the room asking it, switching gender as she went: "I'm switching between men and women because I'm talking to men and women."

Text:
‎{{c1::ما اسم أبوكَ؟ / ما اسم أبوكِ؟}}

Transliteration: {{c1::maa ism abuuka? / maa ism abuuki?}}

{{c2::What is your father's name?}} — to a man / to a woman — she asked the whole room this
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — maa ism abuuka? / maa ism abuuki?

Why: no verb "is" — the question is just what + the name of your father.

Ex: you answer ism abii + the name. Hers: ism abii Elias.

Pitfall: maa goes with a noun, so it is maa here and never hal.

Text:
‎{{c1::أَحسَنتَ / أَحسَنتِ}}

Transliteration: {{c1::aHsanta / aHsanti}}

{{c2::Good job! Well done!}} — to a man / to a woman — she says this to the class constantly
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — aHsanta / aHsanti

Distinguish: -a to a man, -i to a woman. Her words: "you're going to hear aHsant for a man, aHsanti for ladies. You're going to learn those."

Ex: on a student by name [sound:arabic_khouri_ahsant_kyle.mp3]

Pitfall: the capital H is Haa, from the throat.

Text:
‎{{c1::مِن أيّ مدينة أنتَ؟ / أنتِ؟}}

Transliteration: {{c1::min ayy madiina anta? / anti?}}

{{c2::From which city are you?}} — to a man / to a woman — the city version of min ayna anta
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — min ayy madiina anta? / anti?

Distinguish: min ayna anta? asks where from in general; this asks specifically which CITY.

Ex: her own answer — ana min madiinat Dimashq.

Pitfall: ayy and ayna cannot both appear; pick one.
